title: Gravimetric Analysis Practical: Barium Sulfate, Percentage Recovery and Risks | Year 12 Chemistry
originalTitle: Gravimetric Analysis Practical: Barium Sulfate, Percentage Recovery and Risks | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson02.sa.html

Why would a chemist analyse a sample whose sulfate content is already known? To test the method. Carry out a gravimetric sulfate analysis step by step: acidify, precipitate barium sulfate with excess barium chloride, digest, filter, wash until a silver nitrate test stays clear, and dry to constant mass. Calculate the expected mass and the percentage recovery, then judge the results for reliability, accuracy and validity, using a cloudy filtrate as evidence. Includes the risk assessment for barium chloride, silver nitrate and heavy-metal waste. Two practice questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 8, Applying Chemical Ideas.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 8):
"conduct investigations and/or process data involving:
- gravimetric analysis
- precipitation titrations"
This video covers the gravimetric analysis investigation; precipitation titrations are in an earlier video.
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Gravimetric analysis: from precipitate mass to ion concentration. Next: Precipitation titration and gravimetry practice.

title: Precipitation Titration and Gravimetric Analysis: HSC-Style Practice | Year 12 Chemistry
originalTitle: Precipitation Titration and Gravimetric Analysis: HSC-Style Practice | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson01.sa.html
Gravimetric analysis lesson: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson02.sa.html

Practise three HSC-style quantitative analysis questions. Find the chloride in diluted seawater from Mohr titration data, and see why you must scale back through the dilution. Justify which gravimetric result to exclude, then use a one to three formula ratio to find the purity of aluminium sulfate. Then explain why a diluted titrant reads high and a torn filter paper reads low, and why the mean of two wrong results isn't proof of accuracy. Pause and try each question, then work through it step by step. Questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

title: How Do Insulin and Glucagon Regulate Blood Glucose? Two Feedback Loops | Year 12 Biology Module 8
originalTitle: How Do Insulin and Glucagon Regulate Blood Glucose? Two Feedback Loops | Year 12 Biology Module 8
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module8/lesson03.sa.html

After a pasta meal, glucose pours into your blood; overnight, you eat nothing, yet your brain keeps using glucose. Learn the difference between glucose, glycogen and glucagon, how beta and alpha cells in the pancreatic islets detect a change in blood glucose, how insulin lets muscle and fat cells take up glucose and makes the liver store it as glycogen, and how glucagon makes the liver release glucose when it falls. See why two opposing hormones give control in both directions, and why the liver, not the pancreas, is the main effector. Then practise constructing a loop and interpreting a glucose and insulin graph.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 8, Non-infectious Disease and Disorders. Inquiry question: "How is an organism's internal environment maintained in response to a changing external environment?"

title: How Does the Kidney Regulate Water Balance? ADH, Aquaporins and Feedback | Year 12 Biology Module 8
originalTitle: How Does the Kidney Regulate Water Balance? ADH, Aquaporins and Feedback | Year 12 Biology Module 8
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module8/lesson04.sa.html

On a hot day you pass a little dark urine; after a litre of water you pass a lot of pale urine. Learn why the variable your body regulates is blood concentration (osmolarity), how your kidneys filter about 180 litres a day and take most of it back, how osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus trigger the release of ADH from the posterior pituitary, and how ADH puts water channels (aquaporins) into the collecting ducts. See the same negative feedback loop run in reverse after drinking water, and how aldosterone differs: water follows salt. Then practise predicting urine after a salty snack and interpreting a urine output graph.

title: How Do Plants Keep Enough Water? Stomata, ABA and Xerophytes | Year 12 Biology Module 8
originalTitle: How Do Plants Keep Enough Water? Stomata, ABA and Xerophytes | Year 12 Biology Module 8
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module8/lesson05.sa.html

On a hot, dry, windy afternoon a plant can lose water faster than its roots take it up, and it has no brain, nerves or blood. Learn how water leaves a leaf by transpiration, why the same stomata must let carbon dioxide in, how guard cells use potassium ions and osmosis to open and close each pore, and how the hormone ABA closes stomata when water runs short. See the plant's response as a negative feedback loop, the cost of closing, and how xerophytes such as spinifex save water with built-in features. Then practise two HSC-style questions.
